items.title: Why Is Strategy So Difficult?
items.description: O ne might think that the meaning of a word as common as strategy is clear, but it is not. The invaluable Oxford American Writer’s Thesaurus inadvertently captures the confusion: “master plan, grand design, game plan, action plan, policy, program, tactics.” But a master plan is something more specific than a grand design, a policy is what should direct strategy, and tactics exist at a level of intentional action below strategy. The muddle becomes serious when applied to strategy’s original and most important field of human endeavor: war. The roots lie in ancient Greek, which is why stratēgos was the word for “general.” Many weighty works on strategy in war make the basic ideas clear, and yet, as one can see from the badly botched American war with Iran, strategy is acutely difficult. Here we have a war in which the United States has the world’s most advanced technology, highly skilled personnel, and well-trained and -staffed organizations. The U.S. is operating in a theater of war that it has studied for many decades, in partnership with Israel—the most militarily advanced country in the Middle East—as well as, more quietly, most of the Gulf States, and it is receiving the tacit support of countries such as Great Britain. Its enemy is poor and corrupt, and recently lost a large chunk of its senior leadership in a series of bombings and assassinations. But the result is, in important respects, a shocking setback, as Iran continues to throttle one of the world’s most important waterways. This article has been adapted from Eliot A. Cohen’s new book, The Strategist: How to Think About War & Politics . This happened not because America’s weapons malfunctioned, its sailors and airmen were incompetent, or the problems were novel and unanticipated. Rather, America’s battlefield reversals represent a strategic failure of an acutely embarrassing kind. Nor is the issue simply incompetent American political leadership, although that has played its role. The history of strategy is a tale of errors, misjudgments, poor assessments, and inadequate follow-through. It was true of the ancient Greeks, when Athens held the high cards in the Peloponnesian War and lost; it was true of Germany and Japan in the two world wars they launched at times and places of their choosing; it is true of Russia today in Ukraine; it is, for that matter, true of the Iranians themselves, who suffered their own strategic failures against Iraq in the 1980s and Israel in recent years. T he seven core questions of strategy may seem extremely simple, and yet they are rarely answered well. The first is What else is going on? Strategy requires its practitioners to orient themselves to the surrounding environment, for almost never is a country simply facing off against another in isolation. When the Trump administration launched the current round of fighting with Iran, it did so having neglected its environment—indeed, in some ways, having made that environment worse. The U.S. had alienated its European allies, whose active help it needed in keeping the Strait of Hormuz open in the face of mine and surface attacks; it failed to prepare the ground with Gulf allies who would be exposed to Iranian attacks; and it underestimated the extent to which Russia and China had put themselves into a deep partnership with Iran, providing targeting intelligence, the components of military systems, and even some weapons. By fixating on the enemy at hand, the administration neglected the context that had shaped everything else. Governments collect a great deal of intelligence about things that can be counted—tanks, ships, missiles. They do a much worse job of answering the second question, which can be derived from an unlikely classic of strategy: the 1969 movie Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid . Paul Newman and Robet Redford play two relatively nonviolent train robbers in the last days of the frontier. One day, as they are holding up a train, a boxcar door slides open and they are pursued by half a dozen men on horseback. Exciting chase scenes ensue as Butch and Sundance try every trick in their extensive playbook to shake them off, but still the pursuit continues. In bafflement, Butch asks Sundance, “Who are those guys?” It is the second great strategic question, and a subtle one. The two robbers knew how many riders were pursuing them and what weapons they carried. They could probably even tell the breed of horses they were riding. But they did not know what made this band of lawmen so much more persistent and so adept in seeing through their dodges—what motivated them, and what that would mean for Butch and Sundance. That sort of intelligence is difficult to come by, particularly if you do not know that that is the information you need. President Trump and his key advisers likely knew little about the leaders of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, who are now their primary opponents. It is clear that they still cannot fathom how their enemy makes decisions. It is not uncommon for Western leaders to underestimate or simply fail to grasp the ideological or religious motivations of their enemies, and that seems to be part of what has happened in the conflict with Iran. But it seems as well that the administration and its advisers misjudged Iran’s preparedness to launch a protracted, complex war in which it would be outgunned but not necessarily outsmarted. [ Eliot A. Cohen: Don’t ask how this war ends ] The problem is probably reciprocal: If Iran’s leaders have taken the so-called TACO bet—“Trump Always Chickens Out”—they have been repeatedly proven wrong, as indeed have been many of Trump’s domestic critics. They may understand Trump, his motivations, his stock of resolve, and his fears as little as he understands them. Or for that matter, as little as the Israelis understood Yahya Sinwar, the leader of Hamas, even though they had had him in their prisons for 10 years, or as little as Americans understood the calculus of Japanese decision makers in the fall of 1941. Sometimes it is possible not even to know who is in charge on the other side. During most of the Vietnam War, American leaders believed that the charismatic Ho Chi Minh or the experienced General Võ Nguyên Giáp were making the decisions. Later they suspected that it was a collective leadership. In reality, the dominant figure was the colorless first secretary of the Communist Party, Lê Duẩn. In the current war, Trump has frequently expressed his frustration at not knowing who is in charge on the other side. What are we trying to do? is the third and most obvious strategic question, perhaps the easiest to pose and the most deceptive. When critics have gone after the Trump administration over the Iran war, they have usually focused on the supposed unclarity of its goals. They have something of a point, but to a more limited degree than one might think. In truth, the setting of goals, although vital, is a murky and shifting enterprise. Carl von Clausewitz, who in his lifetime witnessed numerous strategic defeats as well as the ultimate victory of the allied coalition over Napoleonic France, taught that war is a continuation of policy by other means. It may be the most important teaching to take away from his classic, On War , and is certainly the most memorable. But if the ultimate objectives in war are political, then they also have political characteristics—that is, they may be vague, inconsistent, and above all changeable. George H. W. Bush famously outlined four objectives for American forces in advance of the 1990–91 Gulf War, in an oft-cited example of strategic clarity. A closer look, however, shows that they were anything but clear. The first objective was ensuring the safety of American citizens in the Gulf—but before the bombs fell, that had already been achieved, because the Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein had released his American and European hostages. American citizens—the soldiers, sailors, airmen, and Marines going into Iraq—were the ones endangered by the war. Expelling Iraq from Kuwait was straightforward enough, but restoring the “legitimate government of Kuwait”—a monarchy backed by a citizenry that included scarcely a quarter of the country’s inhabitants—was not. And as the events of the past 35 years have proven, the fourth objective, ensuring the stability of the Persian Gulf, was a pipe dream. Moreover, some of the objectives the United States pursued either were unstated (stripping Saddam of his nuclear program and setting up the conditions for his overthrow) or evolved only in reaction to events on the ground (protecting the Kurdish population in the north and, to some degree, the Shia in the south). This kind of shift in objectives occurs in all wars. Britain entered World War II nominally to save Poland from Germany. It ended up prohibiting Polish troops from marching in the victory parade in London. The United States invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaeda; it ended up attempting to create an Afghan democratic republic. Considered in this light, the Trump administration’s objective-setting in the Iran war, though messy, is not entirely implausible. Clearly, one objective has been to destroy, or at the minimum badly damage, Iran’s nuclear enterprise; another to limit its ability to threaten its neighbors with missile and drone attacks by dismantling some of its key military industries. A third, and the most questionable, seems to have been to overthrow and replace the regime. That last goal is evidently beyond the current reach of the U.S. military, although the other two have been achieved in some measure. As the war has wound on, the administration has reached for other goals, including the bizarre one of keeping “oil and gas cheap for Americans all over the country,” which Vice President Vance has declared now has primacy over avoiding a nuclear Iran. One problem with the Trump administration’s objective-setting is the president’s foolish insistence that he has achieved more than he has: His repeated use of the word obliteration actually obscures some real, if far from absolute, successes in pursuit of his first two objectives. As for the third, it was always bound to be a reach but was not beyond the realm of possibility. The administration’s real failures have come in setting what were essentially defensive objectives in addition to the offensive ones, above all securing the Strait of Hormuz. For the rest, like many administrations before, it has promised much more than war can ever deliver—think of the hubris of the “war to end all wars,” or the objective of ending tyranny. In democratic societies, the temptation to justify the hazards and sacrifices of war with overblown rhetoric and absurd aspirations usually overcomes the good judgment of political and military leaders alike. [ Read: The Middle East still to come ] What are our means? is the fourth question. At a strictly quantitative level it is usually easily answered by counting tanks, missiles, or ships. But those are often the least important variables in the equation. The real variables are whether organizations can do what we want them to do; whether the technical means we have at our disposal are adequate to the task; and whether, if new challenges arise, we have the resources to meet them. The United States entered the current war with limited stockpiles of its most advanced weapons, limited mine-clearing capabilities, and no frigates whatsoever to escort convoys. It had very little in the way of hardened bunkers for its aircraft in the Persian Gulf, and so suffered some shocking losses on the ground to accurate Iranian missiles (possibly guided by Russian intelligence). And the entire campaign has been predicated on expectations about what bombing could do that were at best highly improbable and at worst totally unrealistic. The administration clearly overestimated what the U.S. military could do, but one has to wonder whether the armed forces also misjudged their own capabilities. Decades of underinvestment in both passive defenses (for example, concrete shelters, underground command posts) and active ones (for example, surface-to-air missile batteries), not any particular decision of the Trump administration, have exposed the U.S. Air Force to high losses. A similar decades-long lack of commitment to the counter-mine-warfare and the escort-of-convoy missions has made the Strait of Hormuz operation so difficult. “Know the enemy and know yourself and in a hundred battles you will not be defeated,” goes the saying of the Chinese general Sun Tzu. But military organizations and their leaders frequently fail to understand themselves, and in particular their own weaknesses. America’s lack of preparedness to conduct classical counterinsurgency warfare in Iraq and Afghanistan cost it dearly in blood, money, and time. Most militaries fail to conduct a sober reckoning with their own deficiencies by examining their lack of resources, organizational preparation, or aptitude. The fifth and sixth questions are What is our priority? and In what sequence should we act? For a country as wealthy and powerful as the United States, these are particularly uncomfortable questions. American leaders often act as though their resources are infinite and few really difficult strategic choices need to be made. That flexibility is one of the blessings (and occasionally the curse) of an astoundingly wealthy and populous country. Economists like the word trade-off —to get this, you have to give up that. The military uses instead phrases such as economy of force or acceptable risk that mask the blunter truth that some things are more important than others. In the current Iran war, it has become clear that getting control of the Strait of Hormuz has never been the top priority—had it been so, the U.S. would have conducted a variety of operations, probably including seizing some of the smaller islands near the strait. Setting priorities can be acutely difficult in war. The best decision Franklin D. Roosevelt made during the Second World War was one of priority. Military and political leaders alike had believed in 1941 that Germany would be a more important enemy than Japan and needed to be tackled first. But the war began for the United States with the Pearl Harbor attack of December 7, 1941. Over the next six months, Roosevelt agreed to the British proposal to invade French North Africa in November 1942. General George C. Marshall, the chief of staff of the U.S. Army, and Admiral Ernest J. King, the chief of naval operations, thought it a strategic error and opposed it, favoring instead an invasion of France in 1943. Roosevelt’s calculation was chiefly political: To sustain domestic support for the “Germany first” policy, American forces had to be in action somewhere in the European theater of operations within a year of Pearl Harbor. He got his priorities right, and Marshall and King, who did not think politically, were wrong. (As it happened, a 1943 invasion would probably have been an operational debacle as well for the untried U.S. Army, but that was a separate matter.) If Roosevelt got priority right, however, he got sequencing wrong. Like most politicians, he did not want to feel trapped by prior decisions—what political scientists call “path dependence.” He believed that he could have the North Africa invasion and still invade France in 1943, and he was wrong. The defeat of German armies in North Africa took longer than expected, and was not completed until March 1943. Sicily loomed as an easy target, and besides, shifting large forces to Britain, particularly before the U-boat menace in the Atlantic was defeated, would take time, so in July the Allies attacked the island and took it. That triggered the fall of the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini; the logical next Allied move was therefore a landing in Italy. That occurred in September 1943, in the immediate aftermath of Italy’s defection from the Axis. And that, in turn, led to a swift German occupation of Italy and an ensuing front in Europe that no one had anticipated. [ Timothy W. Ryback: How Hitler dismantled democracy in 53 days ] Sequencing, then, was only partially under Roosevelt’s control, or anyone else’s for that matter. One thing led to another, and as is so often the case in war, the contenders looked as though they were playing chess one move at a time, seizing an opportunity without fully anticipating the consequences of doing so. The final question is in many ways the most difficult: What is our theory of victory? Or, put more simply, Why do we think this will work? In the case of the Iran war the theory of victory seems to be: We will inflict so much economic pain on the regime that it will give in, either because it will hate to see the Iranian economy ruined or because its people will rise up and overthrow it . But Iran has been suffering self-imposed economic misery for decades, and its leaders, with their own corrupt networks, can live in splendor while others suffer. And as for an uprising, the time to support that would have been when Iranians took to the streets in December and January 2026, before 30,000 were massacred by the Islamic Republic’s repressive apparatus. If there is any theory of victory left for the United States, it is that more reasonable Iranian leaders will replace the extremists—but it would appear at the moment that the hardest of the hard-liners are the ones with the guns. Articulating a theory of victory is no different from constructing a plausible story—the different characters find themselves in a situation, they do this and that, and there is an outcome. In practice, though, such theories are rarely offered in governmental deliberations—and here I speak from personal experience. I saw that play out while sitting in the Situation Room as senior officials discussed sending more soldiers, or diplomats, or aid money to Afghanistan, without anyone quite broaching the question of how the moves under consideration were supposed to lead to success. Such failures are entirely common, as the perusal of archival records confirms. Strategy is chiefly about execution—the exceedingly complicated and difficult task of moving forces from one place to another, guiding them through combat, and responding to unforeseen circumstances. There are ancillary activities—diplomatic initiatives, the public presentation of the reasons for war or expositions of why it is going the way it is, the gathering and deployment of financial and industrial resources. All of this requires serious, detailed, and extremely consequential work. To begin telling a story, or even to ask for one, in such a circumstance can seem frivolous at best, and at worst downright subversive of the efforts officials are investing and the sacrifices soldiers are making. Why is it all so hard? One reason lies in the sheer uncertainty of all wars, in which personalities, contingent events, accidents, bloodlust, shifting political calculations, and sheer good or bad luck play their part. But no less important are the weaknesses of the decision makers themselves. For one, they are often, if experienced, old and suffering the afflictions of age, or if young, inexperienced and either cocky or timid. Historians will parse the records of the Trump administration or, like the cardiologist of the late Vice President Dick Cheney, wonder what it meant that the president was clearly in poor physical and possibly mental health. He would hardly be alone. Prime Minister Anthony Eden launched the Suez operation of 1956 against Egypt’s Gamal Abdel Nasser. At the time, he had been hospitalized with a fever of up to 106 degrees following a set of badly botched gallbladder operations. He had been taking amphetamines and sleeping pills. In a fascinating study of Eden, David Owens, himself a former foreign secretary and a physician, concluded that Eden’s physical health played a large role in the poor decision making that helped produce a major debacle. Roosevelt was on the edge of death in the last year of World War II; Winston Churchill had a heart attack; and Joseph Stalin, in addition to suffering from hypertension, had become increasingly paranoid. John F. Kennedy took a horrifying cocktail of drugs for his bad back and suffered from Addison’s disease. Woodrow Wilson had an incapacitating stroke that left the U.S. government largely in the hands of his protective wife. These are not isolated cases. Even healthy younger leaders may find themselves suffering from acute sleep deprivation and other disorders. A flattering portrayal of President Biden’s national security adviser noted that, during the American withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, Jake Sullivan was getting two hours of sleep a night for days on end. As those who have studied medical residents know, going that short of sleep practically guarantees poor decisions. The psychologist Daniel Kahneman and his colleague Amos Tversky have examined many heuristic shortcuts that distort rational decision making. Almost all of them apply in strategic decision making as well. Take anchoring, our tendency to judge an event, problem, or cost based on some existing piece of information. The trivial case is the extremely expensive bottle of wine put on a restaurant menu with the idea of making the second- or third-most-expensive bottle look reasonably priced. Strategic anchoring occurs frequently. In the run-up to the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, not only Hitler but also his generals concluded that Russia was a fragile giant. They anchored their perceptions on the 1939–40 winter war between the U.S.S.R. and Finland, when 200,000 Soviet troops were killed, wounded, or captured by Finnish militiamen. They paid no attention to the way in which the Soviets had learned swiftly from their failures in that war, and did not account for all of the advantages that Russians would derive from fighting on their own ground. In a similar vein, both the Russian military and Western observers anchored their perception of Ukrainian fighting power in the 2014 and 2015 rounds of conflict in the Donbas as well as the Russian seizure of Crimea. They had discounted, or simply ignored, the improvements in Ukrainian training and equipment since then, or, in parallel with the 1941 case, the differences that would emerge when Ukrainians were fighting to protect their villages and cities from an army that would commit rape and murder with abandon. Strategic decision making is rarely a matter of individual choices; more often it is the result of some kind of deliberation. This is true even in the most extreme totalitarian countries. Stalin called the shots, but Marshal Georgy Zhukhov could get a hearing. This leads to another obstacle to sound strategic judgment: collective pathologies. The phenomenon described by Irving Janis as groupthink applies particularly forcefully to strategic decision making: illusions of invulnerability, collective discounting of warnings, unquestioned belief in one’s own inherent morality, stereotyped views of adversaries, self-censorship, and the exclusion of dissidents, or their reduction to marginal status. Lyndon Johnson heard out George Ball, the in-house dissenter on Vietnam, and then moved swiftly on. These and many other pathologies have beset not only the Trump administration in Iran, but most countries at war. They can be mitigated but not resolved. Formal procedures are less helpful than qualities of character. Of these the most important are empathy, to understand both the enemy and one’s own side; curiosity, because every war is new and distinctive; humility, to accept that one has made mistakes; and above all moral courage, to face facts for what they are and to make decisions accordingly. The president is singularly deficient in all of these aspects. He finds it difficult to imagine the world as seen by others; he seems to be incurious about the important details of military operations; he is far from humble; and if he is averse to anything, it is admitting that he might be wrong. These traits do not seem, moreover, to be confined to him but are shared by many in his administration. [ Listen: The ‘great man’ presidency ] The strategic virtues, to be clear, are rarely found. But they do exist. Churchill, whose courage was justly famous, was a great war leader. He benefited as much, however, from his empathy as from his courage. His great advantage over Hitler, as the historian John Lukacs has shrewdly noted, is that he could imagine what it was like to be Hitler, but Hitler could never imagine what it was like to be Churchill. One cannot study Abraham Lincoln’s conduct of the Civil War without being struck by his curiosity and humility—neither of which interfered with his resolve and decisiveness. Nor is it the acknowledged great figures of history alone who show these qualities: When President George W. Bush made the call in December 2006 to surge forces to Iraq despite the apprehensions of his military and political subordinates, he exhibited considerable moral courage. Israeli Prime Minister Levi Eshkol made a number of decisions in the run-up to the Six-Day War that bought Israel at least a modicum of the support and understanding that it would need from abroad, and which, in very different circumstances, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has so profligately squandered. Some view strategy as so difficult that it is not even worth attempting. These are not only counsels of despair but of nihilism. Some decision makers have shown excellent strategic judgment and used war to achieve their political objectives. The most notable might be Anwar Sadat, the long-underestimated Egyptian president who launched the 1973 Yom Kippur War and used a spectacular early success that could have easily ended in catastrophe to secure the peace he wanted. War is a hideous thing. There are even more hideous things, however, as anyone who has visited the mass graves of Sarajevo or the slaughter field of Bucha in Ukraine will know. A war with Iran now may well be far less terrible than a war launched by an Iran with nuclear weapons later. Moreover, sometimes war is unavoidable: True pacifists are few, and no nation committed to pacifism has survived the predations of a hostile neighbor that is not. The chances are good that anyone reading this article lives in a country that is currently at war, or has been at war, or is closely affected by war. It is a near certainty that they live in a country whose borders have been shaped by war, and quite probably one whose form of government has resulted from war. All of us therefore have, or should have, a keen interest in strategy. Unfortunately, however, its practice will not get any easier in the future. War is spreading to new domains, and employing new and terrible conventional weapons, many capable of acting on the basis of decisions that machines will make in fractions of a second. Nuclear weapons are spreading, and we now face the potential of devastating biological weapons manufactured with the aid of artificial intelligence. The previous experiences and professional knowledge of generals and admirals becomes ever more swiftly obsolete; the hazards of untried political leaders wading through such uncertainty, immensely greater. More countries have the capacity to do terrible things, and are seemingly willing to do so. None of that is an excuse for neglecting the subject that Aristotle thought essential for a citizen. In his Rhetoric , he talks at length about the subjects an orator must master, including “the military strength of his country, both actual and potential, and also the nature of that strength; and further, what wars his country has waged, and how it has waged them. He must know these facts not only about his own country, but also about neighboring countries; and also about countries with which war is likely, in order that peace may be maintained.” Strategy is one of the oldest of subjects. It is powerfully shaped by current events and technologies but best learned through a deep encounter with the history of war. It can be studied but rarely mastered, and it is the domain of both calculation and inevitable error. Of one thing we can be certain: As we look at a world in which violence is not the last resort for many countries and organizations hostile to our values and interests, and may very well be the first, strategy will be needed more than ever. This article has been adapted from Eliot A. Cohen’s new book, The Strategist: How to Think About War & Politics .

items.title: A New Season of Autocracy in America
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts In this new season of Autocracy in America , host Anne Applebaum sits down with leaders in politics, technology, and culture to discuss what can be done now to reverse the slide toward autocracy. The following is a transcript: Anne Applebaum: The midterms mark the beginning of the end of President Donald Trump’s second term in office. Although we don’t know who and what the results will bring, we do know that, regardless of what happens, there will now be opportunities to prevent the further degradation of our democracy. This November, the Autocracy in America podcast is coming back, this time to focus on that recovery. I’m Anne Applebaum of The Atlantic . Join me for interviews with the people who will be leading the charge. I’ll talk with leaders about their plans to work with the administration, to restore international relationships, and to repair the damage done to our economy. I’ll ask what it could look like to retrain and restrain ICE, rescue our cultural institutions, and keep our elections safe. The new season of Autocracy in America arrives Tuesday, November the 10th, and will be available in video and audio. Subscribe on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

items.title: Cameroun : le président d’Interpol Lucas Philippe reçu au Palais de l’Unité
items.description: © DR Le ministre d’Etat, secrétaire général de la présidence de la République, Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh a reçu en audience le 19 octobre, le président d’Interpol. En visite officielle pour la première fois en Afrique, le président de l’Organisation internationale de la police criminelle (Interpol) a été reçu au Palais de l’Unité lundi. Au nom du chef de l’Etat Paul Biya, le ministre d’Etat Ferdinand Ngoh Ngoh a reçu le chef de l’organisation sécuritaire internationale. Il était membre d’une délégation conduite par le délégué général à la Sûreté nationale du Cameroun, Martin Mbarga Nguele. Au cours de la visite, les différentes personnalités ont abordé des sujets dans la perspective de renforcer la coopération entre le Cameroun et Interpol. Les axes de cette coopération ciblent en l’occurrence le terrorisme, la criminalité organisée et les menaces sécuritaires transnationales. Les échanges entre le ministre d’Etat et son hôte ont porté notamment sur la tradition, la modernité, la cybersécurité, la technologie, la jeune génération, en mettant un accent particulier sur les enjeux locaux et les enjeux de la sous-région Afrique centrale. Arrivé au Cameroun le 18 octobre dernier, le contrôleur général Lucas Philippe effectue une visite de plusieurs jours au Cameroun. Le 19 octobre, en dehors de sa visite au Palais de l’Unité, Il a fait d’autres rencontres au Bureau régional d’Interpol à Yaoundé dont celle du secrétaire permanent du Comité des chefs de police d’Afrique centrale, le colonel de police Michel Koua, à qui il a remis un présent. La présence de Lucas Philippe en Afrique s’inscrit en général dans le cadre du renforcement de la coopération policière entre les pays d’Afrique centrale. Ce mardi, Lucas Philippe prend part à la 6è session sécuritaire ordinaire du conseil des chefs de polices de l’Afrique centrale. L’événement se déroule jusqu’au 21 octobre au palais des Congrès de Yaoundé. Composé de 196 pays membres, Interpol est un cadre ayant pour mission de faciliter la circulation sécurisée de l’information et offre un appui aux enquêtes policières, surtout celles qui font au-delà des frontières es pays. Elu à la tête de l’institution en novembre 2025, Lucas Philippe entend faire de cette période le temps de l’action. Cet article Cameroun : le président d’Interpol Lucas Philippe reçu au Palais de l’Unité est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Marché Parc de Matoto : « Nous n’avons plus de recours », les commerçants désespérés interpellent le président Doumbouya
items.description: La crainte de perdre leurs boutiques a poussé des vendeurs et vendeuses du marché Parc de Matoto à manifester dans les allées du marché, ce lundi. En cause : le marquage de plusieurs espaces commerciaux et un délai de 72 heures qui leur aurait été accordé pour quitter les lieux. Face à cette situation, les manifestants, qui affirment avoir multiplié les démarches sans obtenir de solution, lancent un appel au président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya. La tension était perceptible dans cette partie du marché de Matoto. En parcourant les lieux, les commerçants ont scandé des slogans hostiles à l’administration du marché, notamment « bureau zéro, bureau zéro ». Pour eux, le marquage de leurs boutiques fait peser une menace directe sur leurs activités et leurs moyens de subsistance. Selon les manifestants, cette opération serait liée à un projet de libération de l’emprise en vue de la réalisation d’une route. Ils affirment toutefois que ce n’est pas la première fois que leurs boutiques sont marquées et disent vivre cette situation pour la troisième fois. Prenant la parole au nom des protestataires, Mohamed Soumah a rappelé que plusieurs générations de commerçants ont exercé leurs activités sur ce site. Une ancienneté qui, selon lui, rend cette nouvelle menace particulièrement difficile à accepter. « Nous sommes là, il y a des années et des années. C’est ici que nos pères et mères ont vendu. Nous avons ensuite pris la relève. Nous sommes très inquiets aujourd’hui. Ils sont venus cocher nos boutiques en nous disant qu’il faut quitter dans 72h. C’est la troisième fois qu’ils le fassent. Ils nous disent qu’ils le font pour faire aboutir la route ici. Mais, il y a des années que nous sommes là, depuis au temps de feu Alkhaly Mamadou Keita. C’est lui qui nous avait permis de nous installer ici », a-t-il déclaré. « Il est rentré chez lui et en est décédé » : un témoignage qui interpelle Pour illustrer l’impact de ces opérations sur les commerçants, Mohamed Soumah a évoqué le cas d’un de leurs camarades qui, selon son témoignage, aurait été profondément bouleversé par le premier marquage des boutiques. « On avait un camarade ici. La première fois qu’ils sont venus mettre les croix. Il a été tellement choqué, qu’il est rentré chez lui et en est décédé », a-t-il raconté. Les manifestants affirment avoir sollicité plusieurs responsables, notamment ceux du marché. Mais leurs démarches n’auraient pas permis, selon eux, d’obtenir des réponses satisfaisantes. « Nous sommes allés au bureau du marché pour leur en faire cas. L’administratrice dit ne rien savoir. Nous leur avons dit de nous aider. Ils ont dit ne rien savoir et que si nous pouvons quelque chose contre cet état de fait, de le faire », a poursuivi leur porte-parole. Mohamed Soumah affirme également avoir contacté le maire de Matoto, la cellule de communication de la commune ainsi que les personnes qu’il présente comme étant impliquées dans l’opération de marquage. D’après son récit, chacun aurait renvoyé la responsabilité vers un autre interlocuteur, jusqu’au gouvernorat. « Nous avons appelé à la commune aussi. Le maire dit qu’il n’a rien à dire, d’appeler sa cellule de communication. Nous avons appelé la cellule de communication, Monsieur Sanoh dit la même chose et nous a demandé qui était le chef d’équipe ? Nous lui avons dit Monsieur Keita. Monsieur Keita dit que ce n’est pas lui, que c’est le gouvernorat, qui dit aussi n’avoir rien à dire », a-t-il expliqué. Un appel pressant au chef de l’État Face à ce qu’ils considèrent comme une impasse, les commerçants disent ne plus savoir vers qui se tourner. Ils demandent désormais l’intervention du président de la République afin que leur situation soit examinée. « Maintenant, nous n’avons plus de recours. Nous plaidons le Président de nous venir en aide. Nous voulons que les administrateurs du marché quittent ou nous laisse tranquille. Ils ne font pas un bon travail », a déclaré Mohamed Soumah. Les manifestants précisent avoir choisi de rester à l’intérieur du marché pour éviter tout débordement. Ils disent vouloir faire entendre leurs revendications sans recourir à la violence. « Nous ne sommes pas sortis hors du marché pour ne pas qu’on nous brutalise. Nous avons voulu manifester pacifiquement », a-t-il souligné. Une autre interrogation demeure pour les commerçants : pourquoi certaines boutiques ont-elles été marquées et d’autres épargnées ? Les manifestants affirment ne pas avoir reçu d’explications sur les critères retenus pour cette opération. Taxes et ordures : d’autres motifs de mécontentement Au-delà de la menace de perdre leurs boutiques, plusieurs vendeuses dénoncent également les conditions dans lesquelles elles paient les taxes au marché. Selon leurs témoignages, une taxe qui devrait s’élever à 3 000 francs guinéens atteindrait parfois des montants variables. Ces affirmations n’ont toutefois pas pu être vérifiées de manière indépendante. La gestion des ordures suscite également leur indignation. Des commerçants affirment payer leurs taxes tout en étant obligés de rémunérer des jeunes pour débarrasser leurs espaces des déchets. Ils estiment que l’assainissement du marché devrait faire l’objet d’une meilleure prise en charge. Contactée sur place, l’administratrice du marché a reçu notre équipe dans son bureau, mais n’a pas souhaité répondre aux questions devant les micros. Elle n’a pas reconnu les faits qui lui sont reprochés par les manifestants. En attendant une réaction des autorités compétentes, les vendeurs et vendeuses du marché Parc de Matoto restent dans l’incertitude. Mayi CISSÉ L’article Marché Parc de Matoto : « Nous n’avons plus de recours », les commerçants désespérés interpellent le président Doumbouya est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: La Tunisie, 10e pays plus riche d’Afrique en 2026
items.description: Les Seychelles constituent le pays le plus riche d’Afrique en termes de PIB par habitant ajusté selon la parité de pouvoir d’achat (PPA), avec 35 850 US$ en 2026. L’île Maurice arrive seconde avec 35 710 US$, devant le Gabon avec 25 850 US$. La Tunisie, elle, n’arrive qu’en 10 e position avec 15,830 US$. Ces chiffres sont issus de la base de données «Perspectives de l’économie mondiale» ( World Economic Outlook Reports ) du FMI, publiée le 13 octobre 2026. La PPA prend en compte les écarts de prix entre les pays, permettant ainsi une comparaison plus équitable de ce que la production économique permet d’acheter localement. Les chiffres sont exprimés en dollars internationaux courants. Le PIB par habitant mesure la production par personne, et non le salaire moyen ou la richesse détenue par un ménage type. Un classement élevé peut coexister avec une pauvreté généralisée lorsque les fruits de la production sont répartis de manière inégale. Les pays figurant en tête du classement ont atteint cette position grâce à des secteurs d’activité différents. Le tourisme et les services financiers soutiennent les principales économies insulaires. Le pétrole et le gaz jouent un rôle bien plus important au Gabon et en Algérie, tandis que les diamants demeurent un pilier de l’économie du Botswana. Des économies plus vastes, comme celles de l’Égypte et de l’Afrique du Sud, allient une activité manufacturière à des secteurs de services très développés. Le classement ci-dessous compare les données du FMI pour 2026 à travers l’Afrique, en utilisant des valeurs non arrondies pour déterminer les positions. I. B. items.title: As France erupts, Europe's far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections
items.description: The tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat, a reminder of the island’s role as a breadbasket since Roman times. But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting. As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland. Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany’s former Communist east looking for alternatives. The US-Iran war, which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher, has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending. The discontent has spilled onto the streets. In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris’ northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country’s worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire. “Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying,” said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes. “Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. Its terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become.” The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly 100 billion ($112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140 per cent and diesel prices have doubled. In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the “legitimate demands” of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting. “We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted,” he said. Protests erupt across Europe Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and looting stores during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs. In Gela, on Sicily’s southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. “We cultivate the land, we harvest debts,” said one banner. A man throws a plastic traffic cone through a burning barricade amid clashes during a day of demonstrations against the cost of living and rising fuel prices in Paris as part of nationwide protests called by the “Yellow Vests” movement, joined by French high school and university students, Oct 19. —Reuters/File “We are completely at a standstill,” said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers’ representative in Caltanissetta province. “The (fuel) cost has more than doubled.” Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies. Tens of thousands marched through Lisbon on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal’s centre-right government. In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home sparked nationwide demonstrations over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month. Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while large rallies in Albania have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards. The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent. Concerns about purchasing power have become “a major driver of populist politics” across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po. Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe’s mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine. Le pen makes fuel prices a campaign issue The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine . In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April’s presidential election. Macron’s government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets. Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Melenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns. Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen, said Ivaldi. I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time.” Since the Iran war began, Le Pen’s ratings have improved while Macron’s have slipped, according to polling by Elabe. Le Pen’s proposal to sharply cut value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential. Calls to restore Russia ties In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after strong gains in local elections. The cost of living topped Germans’ concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month. German inflation spiked to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9pc, handing ammunition to the AfD to attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The AfD is pushing to restore energy ties with Russia, arguing that Berlins support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europes largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling. Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich. A protestor holds a sign reading “Generations 6-7 redoes May 68” in front of a fire at the Boulevard des Capucines during a demonstration to protest against the “high cost of living”, in Paris, France on October 17, 2026. — AFP Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices … rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them,” he said. These geopolitical shocks are … much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle.” The argument is gaining traction elsewhere. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing competition from National Future, a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci that advocates restoring gas links with Russia. In Poland, one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, concern over energy bills is helping boost support for the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown. Its leader, Grzegorz Braun, has called for a return to buying Russian oil and gas, making the case alongside AfD politicians in Lubmin, where the damaged Nord Stream pipelines land in Germany. I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning, he said.

items.title: L’agroalimentaire tunisien au Sial Paris 2026
items.description: Neuf entreprises tunisiennes, spécialisées dans les secteurs de l’huile d’olive, des dattes et de leurs dérivés, participent au salon Sial Paris, qui se tient du 16 au 21 octobre 2026. Autres secteurs représentés par les 71 entreprises présentes : conserves et préparations alimentaires ; produits de la mer ; produits céréaliers ; pâtes et couscous ; confiseries ; sauces et épices ; produits biologiques ; et plats traditionnels. Cette participation vise à renforcer la présence des produits tunisiens sur les marchés européens, tout en mettant en avant leur qualité et leurs spécificités, indique un communiqué du ministère de l’Industrie, des Mines et de l’Énergie, ajoutant que la Tunisie cherche à accroître le rayonnement de ses produits agroalimentaires traditionnels sur les marchés européens à travers l’initiative «Tunisie, Terre de Saveurs» , s’inscrivant dans une démarche globale de soutien à l’exportation et à l’accès aux marchés internationaux. Cette initiative a pour objectif de mieux faire connaître l’huile d’olive tunisienne — notamment l'huile d'olive vierge extra — ainsi que les dattes «Deglet Nour» et leurs dérivés, auprès des consommateurs et des professionnels européens. Elle vise également à nouer de nouvelles relations commerciales avec des importateurs, des distributeurs et des partenaires économiques. Cette participation a réuni 6 entreprises opérant dans le secteur de l’huile d’olive et 3 spécialisées dans les dattes et leurs dérivés, qui ont proposé une offre diversifiée alliant qualité des produits, un savoir-faire local ancestral et innovation en matière de production, de valorisation et de commercialisation. Une délégation composée de représentants du ministère, du Centre technique de l’emballage et du conditionnement (Packtec) et du Groupement des industries de conserves alimentaires a également pris part à cet événement. Par ailleurs, l'initiative «Tunisie, terre de saveurs» s’inscrit dans les orientations de la Stratégie nationale pour l’industrie et l’innovation, qui vise à renforcer la compétitivité des entreprises industrielles du secteur agroalimentaire et à faciliter leur accès aux marchés internationaux. Le pavillon tunisien au Sial s’étend sur une superficie de 991 mètres carrés, accueillant 71 entreprises opérant dans dix secteurs différents de l’industrie agroalimentaire et de transformation (huile d'olive ; dattes et dérivés ; conserves et préparations alimentaires ; produits de la mer ; produits céréaliers ; pâtes et couscous ; confiseries ; sauces et épices ; produits biologiques ; et plats traditionnels). Cette participation, organisée par le Centre de promotion des exportations (Cepex ) en coordination avec l’ambassade de Tunisie à Paris ainsi que les groupements professionnels des produits de la pêche, des industries de conserves alimentaires, des fruits et des dattes, constitue une occasion de mieux faire connaître la diversité, la qualité et la compétitivité des produits tunisiens. Elle vise également à ouvrir de nouvelles perspectives aux entreprises tunisiennes, notamment par l’organisation de rencontres de partenariat et de coopération avec des acteurs et professionnels français et étrangers, ainsi que par diverses activités parallèles au sein du pavillon tunisien, telles que des séances de dégustation et des démonstrations culinaires ( «cooking shows» ). En marge du salon, plusieurs activités promotionnelles ont été organisées, notamment un atelier au sein d’un institut parisien spécialisé dans la formation aux arts culinaires. Cet événement a comporté une séance de dégustation et de promotion de l’huile d’olive et des dattes (sous forme de « m aster c lass» ), en présence de spécialistes de la nutrition et de la dégustation, ainsi que des représentants d'organismes professionnels et commerciaux français. Par ailleurs, des actions de promotion de l’huile d’olive et des dattes ont été menées dans un espace ouvert au grand public. I. B. items.title: Health ministry gets Momin Agha as 9th secretary in 19 months
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The health ministry has again gotten a new secretary, with the Establishment Division notifying Momin Agha as the new administrative head. Agha, a BS-22 officer of the Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS), is the ninth secretary to be appointed during the tenure of Health Minister Mustafa Kamal, who took the oath in February 2025. According to a notification issued by the Establishment Division on Monday, available with Dawn , Agha “has been transferred and posted as secretary health with immediate effect and until further orders”. A health expert, requesting anonymity, said eight officers had held the post during the past 19 months, with some changes involving repeat appointments. According to him, Nadeem Mahboob remained till March 2025, Nasiruddin Mashood till May 2025, Waqarul Hasan till June 2025, Hamed Yaqoob till Feb 2026, Aslam Ghauri till August 2026, retired Captain Mahmood till Sept 2026, then Fakhre Alam joined, and later Mahboob got additional charge of the ministry for just one day before he was replaced with Agha. When contacted earlier, Kamal had told Dawn that he had nothing to do with the changes of secretaries, as the Establishment Division was empowered to make such decisions. Agha was removed as petroleum secretary in January 2026 and directed to report to the Establishment Division without a further posting. He was replaced by Mirza Nasiruddin Ahmad, who was given the additional charge of the post on a look-after basis pending the appointment of a regular officer.

items.title: Cameroun : six mois après la saisine de l’UA, Maurice Kamto publie le mémorandum sur le changement anticonstitutionnel de gouvernement
items.description: © (DR) L’universitaire et ancien président du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun a accusé le gouvernement camerounais d’avoir opéré un changement constitutionnel en violation des dispositions de la Constitution et des textes internationaux. Mais les sanctions demandées à l'UA restent attendues. Le 20 avril 2026, le Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun a saisi le président de la Commission de l’Union africaine S.E Mahmoud Ali Youssouf. Le parti politique camerounais, par l’entremise de son ancien président Maurice Kamto, accusait alors le gouvernement camerounais d’avoir opéré un changement illégal de Constitution. Et de reporter de manière successive et illégale des élections. D’après le mémorandum daté du 20 avril et rendu public le 19 octobre, le MRC expose les faits de la cause. Le gouvernement camerounais a convoqué le Congrès, lequel a modifié certains articles de la Constitution en instaurant un poste de vice-président qui sera pourvu par nomination. Et dont le titulaire sera le successeur du président de la République. Cette démarche est en violation de l’article 64 de la Constitution en vigueur au Cameroun. Il stipule que « aucune procédure de révision ne peut être retenue si elle porte atteinte à la forme républicaine, à l’unité et à l’intégrité territoriale de l’Etat et aux principes démocratiques qui régissent la République ». Or d’après le parti, elle porte atteinte au principe démocratique de l’élection. Elle va aussi à l’encontre des instruments juridiques fondamentaux de l’Union africaine. En l’occurrence le principe de « promouvoir les principes et les institutions démocratiques, la participation populaire et la bonne gouvernance ». Le parti politique soutient aussi que la violation de l’article 64 de la Constitution camerounaise est une violation de l’article 3 paragraphe 10 de la Charte africaine de la démocratie et de la gouvernance et de l’article 4(p) de l’Acte constitutif de l’Union africaine qui rejette et condamne les changements anticonstitutionnels de gouvernements. A propos du report successif des élections, le MRC accuse le gouvernement camerounais d’avoir violé l’article 15(4) de la Constitution camerounaise en reportant les élections législatives ; l’article 3(4) de la Charte africaine de la démocratie et de la gouvernance en reportant les élections municipales ; l’article 25 du pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques pour les deux types d’élections. Les prorogations de mandats des députés et conseillers municipaux 2025-2026 et 2026-2027 privent les populations de l’exercice de leur droit de vote et portent ainsi atteinte aux principes démocratiques, relève le parti d’opposition. Au regard de ces différents faits, le MRC formule ses prétentions auprès de l’Union africaine. Le parti demande à l’organisation de sanctionner le Cameroun en appliquant des mesures prévues dans des textes. Il s’agit en l’occurrence de la suspension de la participation de l’Etat du Cameroun à l’Union africaine ; des actions diplomatiques en vue du rétablissement des mécanismes constitutionnels de dévolution démocratiques du pouvoir par les élections ; l’engagement à respecter la Constitution et l’Etat de droit et la garantie de non-répétition des actes de changement anticonstitutionnel de gouvernement. Le Parti demande par ailleurs d’interdire les voyages, de refuser la délivrance de visas, de geler les avoirs à l’encontre des auteurs de changement anticonstitutionnel de gouvernement ; sans oublier les restrictions commerciales. Mais, six mois après la saisine de l’Union africaine et le dépôt du mémorandum, le parti d’opposition ne présente pas de réponse de l’organisation continentale. Au pays, l’Etat continue de fonctionner avec les mêmes institutions et les changements décriés par le MRC. Alors que ce parti dénonce un coup d’Etat constitutionnel, d’autres partis malgré tout, demandent au chef de l’Etat de nommer le vice-président. Cet article Cameroun : six mois après la saisine de l’UA, Maurice Kamto publie le mémorandum sur le changement anticonstitutionnel de gouvernement est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Emplois verts : le Minefop vise 12 0000 emplois d’ici 2029
items.description: © DR Placée sous le thème « Entrepreneuriat vert et transition écologique », la 2e édition des emplois verts s'est ouverte lundi 19 octobre 2026 à Yaoundé. Le vert comme gisement d'emplois. Le Ministre de l'Emploi et de la Formation Professionnelle a ouvert officiellement, le lundi 19 octobre 2026 au Majestic Cinéma à Yaoundé, la 2e édition de la Semaine des emplois verts. Organisée du 16 au 20 octobre 2026 par le MINEFOP à travers le Programme de Promotion des Emplois Verts au Cameroun (PPEVC), l'initiative fait suite à la première édition de mai 2024. Elle vise à promouvoir la création d'emplois verts durables par l'entrepreneuriat. Pour la période 2025-2029, le PPEVC ambitionne de créer ou verdir 120 000 emplois décents. Il s'appuie sur 11 projets pilotes – solaire de proximité, recyclage des déchets, aquaculture, reboisement, BTP vert – et une stratégie de financement de plus de 21,15 milliards FCFA. Six filières porteuses ont été identifiées : énergie solaire, recyclage plastique, agriculture biologique et cacao, construction en terre stabilisée, écotourisme et numérique vert. Dans son discours, le Ministre a affirmé qu'« il ne peut y avoir d'emplois verts durables sans compétences adaptées ». Il a rappelé que 5 000 des 25 000 bourses gratuites de l'opération ORFEV-JEUNES concernent les métiers verts et annoncé le lancement des formations 2026/2027 de l'initiative JEME (un jeune, un métier, un emploi). Face aux inondations, à la désertification et à la déforestation, il a appelé à transformer les contraintes climatiques en opportunités, invitant les jeunes à entreprendre et les entreprises à investir dans les compétences vertes. items.title: CITS : ONU Femmes mise sur le numérique pour l’avenir des filles au Cameroun
items.description: © DR Du 15 au 17 octobre 2026 au Palais des Congrès de Yaoundé, ONU Femmes Cameroun a pris part au Cameroon International Tech Summit pour promouvoir une transformation numérique inclusive au service des droits des filles. Le numérique comme levier d'émancipation. C'est le message porté par ONU Femmes Cameroun au Cameroon International Tech Summit 2026. Du 15 au 17 octobre 2026, au Palais des Congrès de Yaoundé, l'agence onusienne a pris part au CITS 2026 à travers le Stand One UN. Une participation qui a permis de promouvoir une transformation numérique inclusive, porteuse d'opportunités pour les femmes et les jeunes. Le sommet a réuni les acteurs de l'écosystème autour de thématiques majeures : compétences numériques, emploi des jeunes, startups, intelligence artificielle, fintech et innovation. Temps fort de cette présence, à l'occasion de la Journée internationale de la fille, ONU Femmes Cameroun et X Code Path ont animé une session sur le thème : « Mon avenir, mon choix : les compétences technologiques au service des droits des filles ». Le constat est sans appel : les compétences numériques sont de puissants leviers pour renforcer l'autonomisation et l'inclusion des filles et des jeunes femmes, tout en élargissant leur accès aux opportunités. En facilitant l'accès à l'information, à l'apprentissage, à l'innovation et aux perspectives économiques, les compétences numériques et technologiques contribuent directement à l'autonomisation des filles. ONU Femmes réaffirme ainsi son engagement en faveur d'un numérique accessible et inclusif, afin que chaque fille puisse apprendre, innover et construire librement son avenir. items.title: Cameroun/ Droit des filles : un atelier pour un agenda national
items.description: © DR Du 19 au 23 octobre 2026, Douala abrite l'atelier du Groupe de travail multisectoriel chargé d'élaborer l'Agenda national pour les droits des filles. Cap sur des engagements concrets pour les filles au Cameroun. Du 19 au 23 octobre 2026, Douala accueille l'atelier du Groupe de travail multisectoriel pour l'élaboration de l'Agenda national pour les droits des filles au Cameroun. La cérémonie d'ouverture a été présidée par M. Nguélé Elie Bertrand, Directeur de la Promotion et de la Protection de la Famille et des Droits de l'Enfant, aux côtés du Dr Patricia Norolalao, Spécialiste du développement des adolescents et du genre à l'UNICEF Cameroun. Un duo État-partenaire technique qui donne le ton de cette rencontre. L'objectif est clair : consolider les six priorités et les 24 engagements déjà proposés, définir des actions concrètes, mobiliser les ressources nécessaires et établir des mécanismes efficaces de suivi et de redevabilité. Il ne s'agit plus seulement d'énoncer des principes, mais de les traduire en actes. Le changement attendu est de taille : doter le Cameroun d'un Agenda national opérationnel, assorti d'engagements mesurables, pour renforcer la protection des droits des filles et favoriser leur participation effective à la vie sociale et politique. Parce que chaque fille mérite de voir ses droits respectés, protégés et pleinement réalisés, l'atelier de Douala se veut le point de départ d'une nouvelle dynamique politique en faveur de l'égalité. Cet article Cameroun/ Droit des filles : un atelier pour un agenda national est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: La lección aprendida de la dana de 2024: las alertas masivas y la prevención son clave para salvar vidas
items.description: Poco después de que la Aemet lanzara el pasado viernes el primer aviso sobre la llegada de una dana a la que bautizó como Adam , la Generalitat Valenciana publicó un post en las redes para recordar a la población qué pasos tenía que seguir en caso de que en los siguientes días recibieran un ES-Alert en sus móviles: “Deja el coche en zonas seguras. No atravieses calles llenas de agua. Evita desplazamientos. Infórmate siempre por canales oficiales”. Eran las 14.27 del 16 de octubre y los primeros efectos del temporal en la región valenciana no llegarían hasta dos días después. En esas 48 horas, el Gobierno autonómico actualizó constantemente en sus redes el temporal e incluso envió un mensaje masivo a los teléfonos para anunciar con un día de antelación el riesgo de inundaciones en el litoral norte e interior sur de Valencia. El resto de publicaciones y Es-Alert han sido precisos, insistiendo a la población en que se subiera a plantas altas en zonas inundables. items.description: PESHAWAR: The Peshawar High Court (PHC) on Tuesday issued notices to the federal and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governments in several petitions challenging the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in the province on Oct 11. PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan moved the PHC on Oct 14 against the measures, requesting the court to declare them unconstitutional. The move to impose emergency and governor’s rule followed heightened tensions between the PML-N-led federal government and the PTI-led KP government. On Tuesday, a two-member bench comprising Justices Ijaz Anwar and Muhammad Faheem Wali took up several petitions, including Gohar’s. PTI leader Shandana Gulzar, the KP Bar Council and leaders of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) have also filed pleas. The bench adjourned the hearing till Nov 10 after hearing preliminary arguments. The court said an order would be issued afterwards, adding that notices would also be issued to Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Usman Awan and the KP advocate general. Barrister Sameer Khosa and PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja appeared on behalf of Gohar. Barrister Sameer argued that a resolution passed by the provincial assembly was mandatory for imposing governor’s rule and emergency. “No approval was obtained from the provincial assembly,” he told the court. Noting that the National Assembly and the Senate approved the action later, the lawyer said, “We have also challenged this in the miscellaneous application.” “The proviso to Article 232(1) states that approval from the provincial assembly is necessary. The word ‘shall’ is used, which means this condition is mandatory,” the petitioner’s lawyer said. He reiterated that the measures had been taken without the provincial assembly’s approval and were therefore illegal. The counsel contended that the situation in KP was not beyond the provincial government’s control. Sameer further contended that the chief minister, Sohail Afridi, and the speaker of the provincial assembly were currently “missing”. Afridi, who has become non-functional as the KP CM, has not been seen since the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency. Federal ministers said a day later that he and some of his cabinet members were in preventative custody . The bench then asked whether the petition included a request for the leaders to be presented before the court or recovered. “Yes, we have made that request in this application,” the counsel replied. He referred to a Supreme Court judgment in the case of ex-CM Pir Sabir Shah, in which the SC had established that the chief minister and the cabinet would continue to function if an emergency were imposed. “In the current case, the chief minister, the cabinet and the advocate general have been stopped from working and rendered inactive,” Sameer said. “Our plea is that the assembly be restored and the chief minister and speaker be released,” he added. Raja also argued that governor’s rule and the state of emergency had been imposed without “fulfilling legal requirements”, calling for the measures to be revoked and the provincial assembly restored. The petitioner, Barrister Gohar, also addressed the bench, arguing that the PTI-led government in KP had always supported the Centre in the fight against terrorism. He went on to claim that 12 MNAs and 14 MPAs affiliated with the PTI had been “picked up”. “Raids are being conducted on the homes of our members; they are being harassed,” he added. “We say that Pakistan comes first, we say that we are one, this country is ours,” Gohar said. Gohar further contended that on Oct 11, deputy commissioners and district police officers had been replaced, as had officers posted at the advocate general’s office. Appearing on behalf of Gulzar, advocate Muazzam Butt also highlighted that the KP Assembly’s approval had not been obtained before the imposition of governor’s rule and the state of emergency. He said that an apex committee had been formed under the National Action Plan (NAP), arguing that it was the committee’s responsibility to assess the security situation in the province. He further argued that responsibility for terrorism could not be placed on the provincial government given the existence of the apex committee. Representing the KP Bar Council, Advocate Babar Khan Yousafzai appeared before the court and adopted the arguments advanced in Gohar’s case. Another petitioner, Advocate Qaiser Shah, supported the imposition of the state of emergency but opposed the proclamation insofar as it imposed governor’s rule. A petition has also been filed by National Democratic Movement (NDM) central and provincial presidents Mohsin Dawar and Bushra Gohar, which was fixed for hearing on Oct 20 (Tuesday). In his petition, Barrister Gohar had urged the PHC to declare the federal government’s decision to impose emergency and governor’s rule in KP “unconstitutional, ultra vires, coram non judice, tainted with malice in law and fact, devoid of objective material, and of no legal effect” and to set aside the proclamation. Filed under Article 199 of the Constitution, the petition named the federation of Pakistan (through the secretaries of the Cabinet Division, law, interior, and defence ministries); the province of KP; KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi; the KP Assembly speaker; and the secretary of the KP Home and Tribal Affairs Department as respondents. Sohail Afridi, who is no longer functioning as the province’s chief minister following the imposition of governor’s rule, was also named as a pro forma respondent. Gohar challenged the “constitutionality, legality and vires” of the October 11 decision, the order deploying army troops to the province, and “all consequential and derivative executive orders, notifications, and bodies” constituted as a result. These included the establishment of the KP Advisory Council and the “arbitrary” detention and removal of Afridi as the lawful chief minister of KP, along with his provincial cabinet, which had been vested with full executive powers under Article 130 of the Constitution. Following the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in the province, the federal government formed an 11-member technocratic KP Advisory Council. PTI reiterates emergency, governor’s rule ‘unconstitutional’ Speaking to the media after the hearing, Barrister Gohar highlighted the “injustice” being inflicted on party workers and supporters, with their MNAs and MPAs picked up, their symbols being removed and demolished, and their houses raided. “We spoke about it in front of the court,” Gohar said. “We have said from day one that this is unconstitutional. Whatever has happened is against the Constitution,” he stressed. “There are no two opinions about it; terrorism is unacceptable in this country. We have condemned terrorism in every form, in every place. We have said everyone should unite to fight against terrorism,” Gohar maintained, adding the party rejects “allegations” of facilitating terrorism. Gohar said the party requested the court to make a larger bench and hear the PTI as soon as possible. “The court has given us the date (Nov) 10. We hope the court decides the matter as soon as possible, because this province, this country cannot stay entangled in this. On one hand, the province is deprived of resources; on the other, it is facing terrorism, and on top of that, its mandate is also being snatched away,” he said. Raja, speaking to the media, termed the imposition of emergency “an attack” on provincial autonomy and democracy. “Provincial assembly resolution is mandatory for emergency,” he said. “Governor’s rule requires the provincial government not to do its work.” “Sohail Afridi is still the chief minister of the province and the cabinet is present,” Raja asserted. Leader of the Opposition in NA Mehmood Khan Achakzai also spoke to the media and said, “We want decisions to be made in the courts. If that does not happen, issues will come out onto the streets.” Achakzai referred to the recent protests in France against the cost of living and inequality , highlighting that the French police did not fire a single bullet. “We will have to protest peacefully against this government too,” the opposition leader reiterated. “The final phase of the uprising has now begun.”

items.title: Feijóo plantea ceder senadores autonómicos a Vox para que no se presente en algunas circunscripciones
items.description: El Partido Popular y Vox aproximan posiciones para concurrir con más fuerza al Senado en las elecciones del 29 de noviembre. Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha confirmado este martes que ambas formaciones negocian en estos momentos para encontrar una fórmula que les permita lograr una mayoría más holgada frente a la papeleta conjunta de PSOE y Frente Amplio. Una vez cerrado el plazo para presentar coaliciones, el viernes pasado, PP y ultras barajan otros planes. En una entrevista en Cope, Feijóo ha apuntado como escenario más plausible el de que los ultras no se presenten en determinadas circunscripciones y que el Partido Popular ceda senadores por designación autonómica como contrapartida. El líder del PP quiere un pacto, mete presión a Santiago Abascal y busca con ese planteamiento controlar los tres quintos de la Cámara alta, lo que le permitiría hacer nombramientos sin tener que pactar con el PSOE. items.title: Kenya: le gourou d’une secte mortifère jugé coupable des meurtres de 190 enfants et d’un adulte
items.description: Un gourou autoproclamé et ses complices ont été reconnus coupables des meurtres de 191 personnes, dont 190 enfants, au sein de leur secte qui encourageait ses disciples à mourir de faim au Kenya pour « rencontrer Jésus ». Des centaines de corps avaient été découverts en 2023 dans l'arrière-pays près des plages de Malindi, dans le sud du Kenya, dans ce qui allait devenir ce que les médias ont appelé le « massacre de la forêt de Shakahola », une des pires tragédies liées à des dérives sectaires dans l'histoire du pays. « J'estime que l'accusation a apporté la preuve de la culpabilité des 29 prévenus dans le meurtre de 190 enfants et d'un adulte », a déclaré la juge Diana Kavedza Mochache au tribunal de Mombasa. Le pasteur autoproclamé Paul Mackenzie, s'est montré impassible lors de la lecture du verdict, plus de trois ans après la découverte macabre de 2023. Cet ancien chauffeur de taxi fait également face, dans des affaires distinctes, à des accusations supplémentaires d'homicide involontaire et de terrorisme. Des proches des victimes, beaucoup originaires de communautés rurales qui se trouvent le long de la côte, étaient présents au tribunal. Francis Wanje, 62 ans, a perdu huit membres de sa famille, dont sa fille et deux de ses petits-enfants, s'est dit auprès de l'AFP « heureux » du verdict la perte de sa famille reste « très douloureuse, et lourde ». « Je sais que les miens ne reviendront pas, mais au moins, les choses ont bougé », après des années d'inaction des autorités, a-t-il confié. Le fils de M. Mackenzie, Dan, 24 ans, qui avait coupé les ponts avec son père et avait lui-même survécu à des sévices, a fait part de son « soulagement ». « Justice a été rendue aux victimes », a-t-il affirmé lors d'une conférence de presse. Le parquet kényan a salué un verdict « historique » dans cette affaire qui a bouleversé ce pays majoritairement chrétien et conservateur. Beaucoup de Kényans ont demandé des réglementations plus fortes pour encadrer les organisations religieuses, notamment après qu'il est apparu que Paul Mackenzie avait été arrêté à deux reprises par le passé, puis relâché. L'avocat de la défense, Lawrence Obonyo, a indiqué que ses clients allaient faire appel. La peine doit être prononcée le 6 novembre. – « Hiérarchie de la mort » – Pendant le procès, le tribunal a écouté plus de 200 témoins des événements qui se sont déroulés entre 2021 et 2023 dans un ranch de 325 hectares dans la forêt de Shakahola. Selon les preuves, M. Mackenzie a « dirigé » la pratique de jeûnes extrêmes pour « rencontrer Jésus », estimant qu'il existait une « hiérarchie de la mort »: les enfants d'abord, puis les adolescents, les femmes ensuite, et enfin les hommes. Le tribunal a également établi que 72 victimes sont mortes de faim, et d'autres des suites d'asphyxie, « de point de compression au niveau du cou » et de « blessures traumatiques à la tête ». Bien que la cause du décès de 110 personnes n'ait pu être établie en raison d'un état de décomposition avancé de leurs corps, le tribunal a estimé, en s'appuyant sur un faisceau d'indices, que l'on pouvait déduire que ces victimes étaient également mortes de faim. La juridiction a également conclu que l'église de Mackenzie présentait les caractéristiques propres à une secte, ayant radicalisé ses membres par le biais de principes fondés notamment sur l'isolement et la domination, tout en rompant les liens familiaux, au point que des mères en sont venues à affamer leurs enfants. « C'est là, en fin de compte, toute la perversité de la radicalisation », a déclaré la juge Mochache. « Ce qui était autrefois impensable devient un acte d'obéissance, et ce qui relevait autrefois de l'instinct devient un péché. » Le gourou avait été arrêté en avril 2023, après que certains fidèles avaient été secourus lorsqu'un groupe de défense des droits humains avait alerté les autorités. L'opération policière avait mis au jour des centaines de fosses communes peu profondes. Une pause dans les fouilles avait dû être décrétée lorsque les morgues locales s'étaient retrouvées débordées par la quantité de corps retrouvés. La Commission nationale kényane pour les droits humains a déclaré en 2024 que le bilan s'élevait à 429 morts, dont certains n'ont toujours pas été identifiés. Mais en janvier, M. Mackenzie a été encore une fois mis en accusation après la découverte de 52 nouveaux corps dans un village voisin. Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Nthenge Mackenzie is accused over hundreds of deaths at his cult compound " width="768" height="546" data-src="/resizer/v2/S5VKD3X55FFF3BW6V4SEHXNP7I.png?auth=f7de7396ae782d9e1067448e39a726cad814c6091c7a6c8532a5212a19f451ed" data-srcset="https://www.dhnet.be/resizer/v2/RM2RQZBATJHLDBFUP5D3JOGGV4.jpg?auth=987ac964123ceb552ef2b411bb721028d179a4b40a5f9adb2cdfb1675787d0c8&width=768&height=546&quality=85&focal=384%2C273 768w" data-sizes="auto" data-optimumx="1" /> Le gourou avait établi « the Good News International Church » (l'Eglise internationale de la Bonne Nouvelle) en 2003, ouvrant des antennes à Nairobi et le long de la côte kényane, sur l'océan Indien, qui ont attiré des milliers de disciples avant qu'il ne décrète leur fermeture en 2019. Il avait été arrêté en 2017 pour des accusations de « radicalisation », puis acquitté, et de nouveau arrêté en 2019 à Shakahola, après le décès de deux enfants, morts de faim. AFP L’article Kenya: le gourou d'une secte mortifère jugé coupable des meurtres de 190 enfants et d'un adulte est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .
